{{Short description|Relationship of a signal transducer}}
A '''linear response function''' describes the input-output relationship of a [[signal transducer]], such as a radio turning [[electromagnetic wave]]s into music or a [[neuron]] turning [[Synapse|synaptic]] input into a response. Because of its many applications in [[information theory]], [[physics]] and [[engineering]] there exist alternative names for specific linear response functions such as [[Magnetic susceptibility|susceptibility]], [[impulse response]] or [[Electrical impedance|impedance]]; see also [[transfer function]]. The concept of a [[Green's function]] or [[fundamental solution]] of an [[ordinary differential equation]] is closely related.

==Mathematical definition==

Denote the input of a system by <math>h(t)</math> (e.g. a [[force]]), and the response of the system by <math>x(t)</math> (e.g. a position). Generally, the value of <math>x(t)</math> will depend not only on the present value of <math>h(t)</math>, but also on past values. Approximately <math>x(t)</math> is a weighted sum of the previous values of <math>h(t')</math>, with the weights given by the linear response function <math>\chi(t-t')</math>:
<math display="block">x(t) = \int_{-\infty}^t dt'\, \chi(t-t') h(t') + \cdots\,.</math>

The explicit term on the right-hand side is the [[leading-order|leading order]] term of a [[Volterra series|Volterra expansion]] for the full nonlinear response. If the system in question is highly non-linear, higher order terms in the expansion, denoted by the dots, become important and the signal transducer cannot adequately be described just by its linear response function.

The complex-valued [[Fourier transform]] <math>\tilde{\chi}(\omega) </math> of the linear response function is very useful as it describes the output of the system if the input is a sine wave <math>h(t) = h_0 \sin(\omega t)</math> with frequency <math>\omega</math>. The output reads

<math display="block">x(t) = \left|\tilde{\chi}(\omega)\right| h_0 \sin(\omega t+\arg\tilde{\chi}(\omega))\,,</math>

with [[Amplifier|amplitude gain]] <math>|\tilde{\chi}(\omega)|</math> and [[phase shift]] <math>\arg\tilde{\chi}(\omega)</math>.

==Example==
Consider a [[damped harmonic oscillator]] with input given by an external driving force <math>h(t)</math>,

<math display="block">\ddot{x}(t)+\gamma \dot{x}(t)+\omega_0^2 x(t) = h(t).  </math>

The complex-valued [[Fourier transform]] of the linear response function is given by

<math display="block">\tilde{\chi}(\omega) = \frac{\tilde{x}(\omega)}{\tilde{h}(\omega)} = \frac{1}{\omega_0^2-\omega^2+i\gamma\omega}. </math>

The amplitude gain is given by the magnitude of the [[complex number]] <math>\tilde\chi (\omega ),</math> and the phase shift by the arctan of the imaginary part of the function divided by the real one.

From this representation, we see that for small <math>\gamma</math> the Fourier transform <math>\tilde{\chi}(\omega) </math> of the linear response function yields a pronounced maximum ("[[Resonance]]") at the frequency <math> \omega\approx\omega_0</math>. The linear response function for a harmonic oscillator is mathematically identical to that of an [[RLC circuit]]. The width of the maximum, <math>\Delta\omega ,</math> typically is much smaller than <math>\omega_0 ,</math> so that the [[Quality factor]] <math>Q:=\omega_0 /\Delta\omega</math> can be extremely large.

==Kubo formula==
The exposition of linear response theory, in the context of [[quantum statistics]], can be found in a paper by [[Ryogo Kubo]].<ref>Kubo, R., ''Statistical Mechanical Theory of Irreversible Processes I'', Journal of the Physical Society of Japan, vol. ''12'', pp. 570–586 (1957).</ref>  This defines particularly the [[Kubo formula]], which considers the general case that the "force" {{math|''h''(''t'')}} is a perturbation of the basic operator of the system, the [[Hamiltonian function|Hamiltonian]], <math>\hat H_0 \to \hat{H}_0 -h(t')\hat{B}(t') </math> where <math>\hat B</math> corresponds to a measurable quantity as input, while the output {{math|''x''(''t'')}} is the perturbation of the thermal expectation of another measurable quantity <math>\hat A(t)</math>. The Kubo formula then defines the quantum-statistical calculation of the [[susceptibility (disambiguation)|susceptibility]] <math>\chi ( t -t' )</math> by a general formula involving only the mentioned operators. <!-- It is <math>\chi ( t -t' )= -(i/\hbar )\cdot \langle [\hat{A }(t-t' ),\hat B(0)]\rangle_{\text{thermal expectation}},</math>  where the brackets mean the thermal expectation value, the expression [...&nbsp;,&nbsp;...] the quantum [[commutator]], and <math>\hat{A(t-t')}</math> must be evaluated in the quantum-mechanical [[interaction picture]] with the Hamiltonian <math>\hat{H}_0.</math> -->

As a consequence of the principle of [[Causality (physics)|causality]] the complex-valued function <math>\tilde{\chi }(\omega )</math> has poles only in the lower half-plane. This leads to the [[Kramers–Kronig relations]],  which relates the real and the imaginary parts of <math>\tilde{\chi }(\omega )</math> by integration. The simplest example is once more the [[damped harmonic oscillator]].<ref>De Clozeaux,''Linear Response Theory'', in: E. Antončik et al., ''Theory of condensed matter'', IAEA Vienna, 1968</ref>
==Nonequilibrium linear response formula==
Linear response theory has versions for nonequilibrium processes for open systems where there is no detailed balance but a steady driving or agitation is applied. A small perturbation of these driven or active systems gives rise to a response in violation with the equilibrium expressions. A possible methodology proceeds via path-space ensembles where the probabilities of trajectories are evaluated; see e.g.<ref>Christian Maes, "Frenesy: Time-symmetric dynamical activity in nonequilibria", ''Physics Reports'' '''850''', 1–33 (2020).</ref> The resulting response formulae have an entropic part (similar to the detailed balance case) and a frenetic part. The latter involves the correlation of the (excess) [[Frenesy (physics)|frenesy]] (due to the perturbation) with the observable. In detailed balance, the two contributions merge and reproduce the Kubo and [[Green-Kubo]] formulae. Out of detailed balance, the frenetic contribution is responsible for the possibility of negative heat capacities and mobilities, and they do not longer measure a fluctuation, e.g. in terms of a variance of the energy or of the current.
